why: Harie is a working Japanese farming settlement whose water arrangement is a nationally designated Important Cultural Landscape, and this page states both facts our question needs in the community's own words - the settlement on one bank of the river, its own stream through the middle of the district. Its limits: no date for the arrangement it describes, so it is evidence of the FORM and not of its age; and the springs that make Harie what it is are a local hydrology, not the general case.

It gives the plain distinction between a channel that brings water and one that takes it away, which is the distinction the map's two ditch classes draw. Its limits are no history of when the two were separated and nothing on where drainage went, so those rest on other sources; and that the page itself says a supply channel today often carries rainwater and household waste water too, so the clean two-way split is the older form rather than the present one.

Its opening sentence states the cutting cycle of the konara fuel woods of Niigata as 15 to 30 years. The article is about a modern trial; the old practice is one line of background, and it has three limits. "Formerly" is not dated: most plausibly it means the fuel and charcoal woods worked until the switch to oil and gas in the 1950s and 60s, and it is not shown to be an Edo-period or earlier practice. The figure has no source behind it. And it describes one Japanese prefecture. We use it as the rough length of a coppice cycle, not as a measured premodern figure.

It fixes what the Japanese word for a log bridge meant: a log laid across and nothing more (the Nihon Kokugo Daijiten says one log, and gives a second sense, any bridge built of logs). That this was the simplest crossing is our reading of "nothing more"; the dictionaries compare it with no other crossing, and a ford or stepping stones are simpler still. It is a definition only, from modern dictionaries - it gives no size, no place, no date beyond the word's first appearance in writing (1190), and nothing on who laid one; the only water it names is a narrow valley stream (細谷川) in the earliest quoted poem.

It is the one read account of which paddies carried a winter crop, where and when, which decides whether a map's paddy ground was bare or sown over winter. It is a signed encyclopedia entry, a summary that names two primary sources (a 1264 shogunate law, and the travel diary of the early Muromachi Korean envoy Song Hui-gyeong, the Roshodo Nihon Koroku, on a paddy near Amagasaki cropped three times a year); its northern limit is the one measured before the Second World War, not an Edo line; and it names the Kyoto-Osaka region and the Inland Sea coast as where the practice grew in the Edo period without giving shares. Its list of the crops sown after the rice is undated and partly modern: it includes potatoes, which reached Japan only around 1600, and onions, grown there only from the Meiji period. The winter crops for a map of the Edo period or earlier come from its history section instead: barley, and from the early Muromachi period soybeans, adzuki beans, buckwheat and foxtail millet.

It states plainly what the channels were for and where the storehouses stood, which is the arrangement our wharf granaries copy. Its limits are that it is used beside the encyclopedia article it agrees with, and that its subject is the shogunate's central granary of sixty-seven storehouses, from which only the form and not the scale transfers to a provincial seat.

It records flowers sold from the country into a city's houses in the Edo period, and when growing flowers as a farm crop began there. It relies on a growers' association anniversary book and on legend. For the Edo-period sales it says only that a record exists, without naming it; the one period text it quotes, Matsudaira Sadanobu's 1792 travel diary, says narcissus bloomed in great numbers near Hota; the page reads that as showing they were already grown there, but it shows no sale. So the sale into Edo's houses is the page's claim, not a record we have seen; it contradicts itself on when market growing began, since its history section names Meiji-era lilies and peonies before the Taisho start its headline gives.

It gathers several dictionary and encyclopedia entries on the office, one of them signed by Kodama Kota, a historian of the Edo post-station system, and it says where the office stood and that it could be part of the house of the toiya, the station's chief official (not the village headman). Its limits are that these give no evidence, so "one or two to a station" is a generalization, not a count; that it describes an office, not a yard: it names no stable and no waiting ground; and that its crowd of hundreds of horses and thousands of men is the extreme of a great passage on the shogunate's main highways, with relief levies called in, not an ordinary day at a small station.

It is the only readable source that sizes a Japanese stable. Its limits are that these are by a student of the folk house; that the stable it sizes is the farmhouse's, not an inn's or a relay's, and its warrior-house stable is given only by its form and length; that its 3 m square is the stall for one horse (the usual size by one article, the narrow Kinki size by the other), with the stables of the long-wintered northeast and of horse-breeding districts much larger; and that it describes the folk house as surveyed in modern times, dating only the northeastern house-stables to the Edo domains and noting that Meiji encouragement of horse-breeding for the army came after them.

The rural town is a Japanese market town below the castle town, and the article describes its plan in words. Its standing in for a county seat is this project's analogy, not the article's: the rural town was legally a village and mostly a center of trade rather than of government (a few, such as Kurashiki and Hirano, held an intendant's or a lord's office), where the Chinese county seat was a magistrate's walled seat. Its plan sentence rests on a modern national town-planning guide rather than a history and speaks of most cases, not all; its planned, moated exceptions are temple-precinct towns and medieval cities, mostly in the Kinai. Its town "every few kilometers" is a loose phrase, not a measured spacing, taken from Wakita Osamu's entry in a Heibonsha encyclopedia. It describes Settsu and Kawachi near Osaka and Hirano in the late seventeenth century, the cotton-growing core of what the article calls Japan's most economically advanced region: a dense case, not a typical one. The article says such towns formed elsewhere later, around 1690-1730.

It names the form and what it was for - a boundary mark, a windbreak, a check on soil washing off - and says a household sold what it did not drink. Its sentence on bund tea rests on one footnote: a page on what appears to be the old website of the Miyoshi town history and folk museum (Saitama, on the Musashino upland), which the article also lists under its external links. The form it cites is one region's dry-field practice. It dates bund tea only as one of the old forms common before the change after the Second World War to cuttings and bred cultivars. So it shows the form in the modern era, with surplus shipped to wholesalers, not that it existed in the Edo period or earlier. It gives no count, spacing or row length. It carries the form and its purposes, not a date or a number.

It gives the mound's size, that it was built in pairs either side of the road, and which trees stood on it and in what shares - the great roadside tree a traveler met on the way to a village. Its numbers rest on weak sources: the size (5 ken square, 1 jō high) comes from a 2005 popular trivia paperback, and the species shares (enoki 55%, pine 27%, cedar 8%) come from a web page of a foundry-engineering society that gives no survey, date or basis. The article also converts 1 jō to 1.7 m, when it is about 3 m. The size is the prescribed standard, and surviving mounds vary. The shares are for the five main highways, and the Nikko road differed (cedar led there). The mounds stood on the shogunate's trunk highways, so a village met one only if it lay on such a road. This is Edo Japan's own institution standing in for the setting's roads; the shares are used for which trees were usual, not as exact figures.

It shows a province keeping one combined shrine, the sōja, where the gods of all its shrines were worshipped together, near its provincial seat of government, with a town later grown around it. Its limits: its history rests on the shrine's own leaflet and a gazetteer (Heibonsha's 岡山県の地名); the sōja is the governor's combined shrine, not the province's first-ranked shrine (the ichinomiya, which stood elsewhere), so it stands for a capital's official shrine and not the province's greatest one; the sōja is an institution of the ancient provincial government, older than the castle towns, and the town around it grew in the Edo period as a shrine-gate and post town after the 1687 rebuilding, not as a seat of government; one shrine; no precinct area is given.

Its section on Japan says that until modern times the ordinary road was earth trodden hard by people and horses, and gravel was confined to main roads - the one readable statement found of what a lesser road was surfaced with. The sentence itself carries no footnote. The section's footnotes, from the next sentence on, cite Suzuki Satoshi's 『道-古代エジプトから現代まで』 (1998), but the article does not tie this claim to it. It bounds the rule only as "until modern times" for Japan as a whole, with no period or region within Japan.

It explains why an in-between station was forbidden to lodge travelers - the post towns bore the official relay and the shogunate protected their inns - and that its street was lined with shops. It has carried a banner since April 2013 saying it lacks sources: the ban on lodging itself is footnoted only to two Japanese dictionaries (Daijirin and Daijisen), and its reasons - the relay burden, the shogunate's protection of the post towns' inns - are unsourced, so they carry the general picture and not a firm rule. The article itself says the absence of inns, porters and a relay office was nominal, in name only (名目上・表向き), so the ban is the official rule, not always what a traveler found; and it notes exceptions, such as a former station like Kikugawa, where lodging was allowed when the Ōi River was closed.

It defines the landing and names which Tokaido rivers were forded and which ferried. They carry the shape of the practice, not a date. The encyclopedia names only the crossings it calls well known, not every one. Its split between forded and ferried rivers is given once for the whole Edo period, though how a river was crossed changed over the period (the Rokugo was bridged until 1688 and ferried after).

It shows what a domain-built school held besides its Confucian hall. It was a school for commoners in the countryside, not the domain's school for samurai in the castle town, and the article itself calls it unmatched in its care and scale, so it is the finest case, not a typical one. Most of it is cited to the school museum's display boards and a pamphlet handed out at the site. Its list of protected buildings is what survives, not all the school held: the student dormitories, the writing hall and the teachers' lodgings were taken down after the school closed in 1870. (Its counts of 24 and 25 protected structures agree: the 25 protected in 1938 included the lecture hall, which was made a National Treasure on its own in 1953.)

A dated, measured early-Edo hall of a provincial temple (18.7 m by 11.8 m, 1629) is one size anchor for a temple's main hall. It was built as a Zen abbot's quarters (hōjō), a residence and reception building with a room-grid plan, and only later became the main hall; so it gives the size of that kind of building, not of a worship hall such as a Buddha hall or kondō, which in a large precinct could be bigger. The entry gives only the measurements and roof; it says nothing about the temple's rank or wealth, so it cannot show on its own whether this was a substantial temple or an ordinary one.

It is a surviving instance of the quiet road town the record sets against the busy highway's, thatched and farmhouse-like. It is one mountain station in the snowy north-east; its "half farming" claim rests on a paper it cites (Nakao Chiaki, 2010, Nara Women's University, hdl:10935/1629), and the page hedges it as what the station is thought to have been. That character was not how the station began: it opened about 1643 with a honjin and waki-honjin on the Aizu lord's procession route, and turned half-farming after the processions were stopped in 1680 and the road was cut by the 1683 Nikko earthquake. What stands today is partly a Meiji change and partly a modern restoration: the water channel ran down the middle of the road until 1886, when it was split to both sides and the road widened; roofs went to tin from the 1950s-70s and were re-thatched under preservation after 1981; the asphalt was taken up to restore a dirt road; and the honjin is a 1984 rebuilding. It does not date the houses, or say how common such a town was.

A signed encyclopedia entry covering Japan in general and the period before the hand pump, which is the period the maps draw. It names the forms without saying where or when each prevailed, cites no period record, and gives no dimensions. The bucket well lasted until the hand pump and piped water, which is modern, so the forms it describes were probably recorded by folklorists in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries; that they are Edo or older is our inference, not the entry's statement.

It places the outcaste head's seat at the city's northern edge beside the river, in English. It is Wikipedia's article, copied, and the passage cites nothing even on Wikipedia, so it carries the general layout and not a checked fact. It puts Danzaemon only "nearby" the path and canal to the Yoshiwara (the path starts at the Sumida bank), not by the river itself. It describes one city, the capital, and gives no reason for the placing.

It gives the street's Edo-period origin - a right to trade on the approach granted to local residents who owed the temple the sweeping of its precinct - and its two Edo-period halves, twenty water teahouses nearer the inner gate and shops selling toys, sweets and souvenirs nearer the outer one. Its count of about 90 shops on about 250 m is the present street, rebuilt in 1885 and 1925 and restored after its interiors burned in the Second World War, not an Edo count, and Sensoji was the greatest pilgrimage temple of the shogun's capital. Its Edo-period account comes from the shopkeepers' association's own page and a tourist site, not from period records. It gives the founding only as sometime between Genroku and Kyoho, or by one account about 1685. So it is good for the shape of the street, not for exact dates.

It is the one fully preserved prefect's yamen in China, the tier between a county and a province, so its dimensions are a direct measure of one regional governor's compound - one prefecture's site, not a size the statutes fixed for every prefecture. It gives the site's outer dimensions without saying how they were taken, and describes the compound as rebuilt through 1901 and then altered again: Republican offices from 1913, further additions after 1932, and a guesthouse and staff housing compound from 1965. So the extent it gives is the site as it survives, not surely its Qing extent. Another readable page gives the same site twice the area.

It is the historical form of a warrior's house in the countryside: the residence set among its own paddy, mostly well-established fields, the land where the lord's hold was strongest - the nearest real thing to the setting's samurai country estate. It describes the medieval period, before the Edo-period move of samurai into castle towns, and it is a page of short dictionary and encyclopedia entries (the Nipponica one signed by the historian Kimura Shigemitsu). It gives no typical size for the fields and no distance from the house. The only figures it has are a planting song's praise of a two-tan kadota and one lord's seizure of over a hundred chō under the name, and neither measures the usual form. So it carries the placement and not a figure.

It gives the Japanese earth bank's height and parts, which is what a Japanese-model town enclosure is drawn from. Its 2 to 3 m height is a general range for castle banks, measured from the inside of the enclosure (the outer face, down into the moat the bank's soil was dug from, stands higher), not a measured town bank, and it gives no base width.

It separates the domain's border post from a town's own watch, which is what keeps a border post off a town map. Few inline citations, one of them a television program; it describes the institution, not any post's buildings.

It says where such a market was held - at the gates of temples and shrines, at landing places and road junctions, and near an estate's office or its steward's residence - and that a region's market days were set against its central market's so neighbors did not compete. It is a set of short dictionary entries: the Nipponica entry is signed by Sasaki Ginya, a historian of medieval markets, but the staggering of market days comes only from the unsigned Yamakawa entry, which names no market and no schedule, so it carries the pattern and not a spacing or a count. It describes the medieval market, before the early-modern market town; it gives no size of a market ground.

It names the ground a Japanese shrine festival keeps outside the shrine - one or several stops along the procession's route, or the place it sets out to reach - and says what that ground may be: an existing shrine building (the shrine's original seat, a subsidiary shrine, the shrine of the god's consort), a temporary altar set up on the god's old site, or the house of the parishioners' head (tōnin). It is a short encyclopedia article with no references, flagged as needing sources since 2017. It supports the outline of the practice, not any figure, and gives no dates and no size. Signed dictionary entries on Kotobank (日本大百科全書, 世界大百科事典) date the practice to the Heian period and give its distances from the shrine; this article does neither.

It is the one readable page that places named castle towns' quarters on the ground - Matsumoto's at the castle town's entrances in 1588, Ueda's likewise in 1649 - and gives their local name, machi-hanare. It cites no source at all for these lines; its one footnote supports a different point. What it says of Shinano is one province's policy, and the article itself says the word's meaning differed region by region: Osaka's chori headed large hinin settlements, not small quarters at a town's gates. Its only household figure, also uncited, is that when they were founded the Shinano quarters were overwhelmingly settlements of one to a few households.

It is the one page read that sizes a samurai archery ground and says where it stood. Its figures are the standard it says warrior houses set, not a survey of real ranges. A breadth of one bow-length is at most a single shooting lane; the entry does not size the shooting hall or the ground around it. The entry is short and names no town. The page's second sense is the Edo paid archery parlour: from about 1789 it shot at 7.5 ken (about 13.5 m) in temple precincts and amusement quarters, and it was a front for unlicensed prostitution. That parlour is another institution, and none of its figures or places size the samurai ground.

It describes Edo-period Japan directly and gathers the standard figures, naming the survey behind them. Its limits are that it footnotes none of its counts: the national count, the Edo count and the ten to a hundred pupils per school carry no citation; that its national count (16,560) differs by a thousand from other retellings of the same survey (15,560); that the survey looked back from the 1880s and recorded only the schools localities reported, and is generally read as an undercount, so its counts are floors; that its Edo figure (400-500 large schools, 1,000-1,300 in all) is an estimate for the largest city, not a town of ours; that its masters' breakdowns are for early-Meiji Tokyo (a ranking, not counts) and one small Bingo district of seven schools; and that it gives no provincial castle town's count.

It is the one reference found that says who fought fire in a village. Its limits are that it is the Sekai daihyakka jiten section, signed by Oguma Makoto; that its village passage is two sentences, which name the groups and their night rounds with wooden clappers and iron staves but describe no firefighting apparatus; and that it dates the practice only as lasting "until the modern era", without naming a period or a region.

It is a domain's own time bell described as the castle's bell, placed at one spot in the town, rung twelve times a day in the late Edo period. In 1687 four ringers held the duty, whom Saitama City's own page only supposes were ashigaru and chūgen; by 1828 the duty had passed to the headman (nanushi) of Shibue-machi, a townsman. Its facts all come from Saitama City's cultural-property pages, the closer source. Neither says the town had no other bell: that this was the town's single time bell is our reading of their silence, not their claim. It is one small domain, and the tower that survives is a rebuilding of 1852-1866 after a fire in the Tenpō era.

It gives the common size of a household storehouse, about 2 by 3 ken (3.64 by 5.46 m), in the words of a plasterer who builds them. Its limits are that it is quoting one craftsman, not a survey; that his figure is in the present tense, the common size of the storehouses he builds and restores today (new ones among them, often fitted out as one six-to-eight-mat room), not a count of old ones; that it gives no source, period or class for the figure and converts the ken at the modern 1.82 m, where the period ken varied; and that it speaks of storehouses in general, framed by wealthy provincial houses, not a samurai household's.

It is naming no source for its dates, and its account of the start (a Muronoki farmer's initiative) differs from the ALIC report's (the lord's order). It is used only for its date of 1811 for the domain's own lotus enterprise, which places a lotus district under a domain before the Meiji era; it gives no area.

Its length and its 1790s house count come from Edo-period documents, and the 1843 count from the same period, so a post town's length and houses can be set against each other without a modern extent. The 1843 figures carry no named source on the page, and neither count says how many houses fronted the road.

It names the street-facing earth floor as the finishing room, where guns were assembled and adjusted, and says the forge now shown was newly built from a Meiji-period drawing, so it marks the forge as a reconstruction (it calls the counting desk in the shop room a re-creation too); it does not say which of the rest of the house is original and which was restored in the repair finished in 2024. Its limits: its heading calls the rebuilt forge an Edo one while its text rests it on a Meiji picture; it gives no size or place for the forge building; and it describes one exceptional house - by its own account much the largest in its quarter, 17.5 ken (about 35 m) across after growing from 6 ken in the late seventeenth century, home to the leading Sakai maker and still making guns in the Meiji era - so its finishing room, which the page itself says ordinary machiya lacked, is one leading gunsmith's arrangement rather than a typical town smith's, and the page does not say when the room took that use.

It says where the charcoal is cooled: black charcoal inside the kiln, sealed so that no air enters, and white charcoal drawn out red-hot and smothered beside the kiln under a damp powder of ash and river sand; it says the white-charcoal method is held to have taken its settled form in the Heian period. It describes the craft as practiced today and dates each method only as tradition: the black-charcoal method as largely settled in the Muromachi period, the white-charcoal method in the Heian period, both improved since (binchotan is an Edo invention). Before them, charcoal was burned in an earth-covered pile, and it does not say how that was put out. It says nothing of where charcoal was kept once it left the kiln.

It says that the shrine, as guardian of the Sumida river, drew the faith of those who worked on the river, water-transport operators and boat inns among them, which is a water god kept by the river trades of a great city. It cites no sources of its own, so nothing it says can be traced back to evidence. It gives that faith no date, calling its founding unknown beyond a legend that Minamoto no Yoritomo founded it, and dating only its renaming in 1872. It shows that the shrine stood in Edo (it carries Hiroshige's print of the Suijin grove from his One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, and lists a signpost written by the late-Edo writer Santo Kyozan), but not when the boatmen's worship began, so it cannot by itself place that worship before the modern period. And it is one shrine in one great city, standing in for a general pattern.

It counts the trees of one water-mouth grove as it stands today and gives their ages: over a hundred trees, most over five hundred years old, which puts a grove of that size at the village mouth well before 1912. It is one grove in one village; the village was bought whole by a tourism developer in 2009, its people moved down the hill, and it is now a scenic resort, so the grove it counts stands in a managed tourist site; it gives no area, does not say how the ages were found, and says nothing of trees lost or planted since.

It attests the clerks as entrenched local staff, the official's dependence on their knowledge and their enrichment out of the revenue they handled, which is the clerk this page's county runs on. Its thousand is not a count. It is the critic Hong Liangji's complaint of the 1790s, "今州縣之大者，胥吏至千人" (in translation, "now in the largest departments and counties the clerks reach a thousand"), which the article quotes without a footnote; its notes add only Hou Fangyu's seventeenth-century "每县殆不止千人" (in translation, "each county has hardly fewer than a thousand"). Both are polemics against the clerks, not counts: Hong's is of the largest counties in the Qianlong-Jiaqing years, when county populations had swelled, and Hou's, of the mid-seventeenth century, is a flourish about every county. The article's only empire-wide figures, about 350,000 clerks central and local under Tang Xuanzong and about 440,000 in the Northern Song Yuanyou years, would average a few hundred at most to a county if spread across the empire, well below a thousand. The article gives no statutory quota of clerks to set against the number, so we take it as the upper end of what period critics complained of, not a figure for an ordinary county.

It gives the grove as the screen at the village's rear, the back-hill 龍座林 planted against wind and wash, and the useful trees planted in it; its detail is Hong Kong's, giving a grove area of about 600 sq m to one hectare below 100 m elevation, to be read beside the survey this page's grove sizes rest on.

It gives, in English, the temple quarter at the rim of the castle town with its precincts counted as part of the defenses, which is what puts the teramachi where our maps put it. It also describes the townsmen's houses standing along the road without gaps, on a smaller area than the samurai's. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary at one further remove: the English is a machine-translation research corpus (the bilingual corpus of Wikipedia's Kyoto-topic articles made by NICT, Japan's National Institute of Information and Communications Technology), a frozen snapshot rather than the maintained article, which is why it reads as it does; and that two other entries in this registry point at the same article and at the Japanese original it translates, so the three cannot corroborate one another.

Whether servants show up on a city map as their own little houses or as nothing at all turns on whether they lived in their master's compound or in their own, and this article answers that directly: they were live-in staff on term contracts, hired through labor brokers as a household needed them. That the brokers stood in the merchant quarter is our inference, not the page's statement. It is about people and their conditions of employment, not about buildings, and it describes a specifically Edo-period arrangement, so the drawn form of the quarters they occupied comes from other sources.

We use it for the shape of the castle town's zoning - merchant wards forming strips along the main roads that separated one group of samurai from another, and the precise spatial arrangement that kept samurai and townspeople apart - which is what the ring-and-strip layout of our capitals is drawn from. Its limits are that it is a tour operator's essay unsigned and without references; that the same zoning is better anchored in the Japanese encyclopedia article; and that it says nothing about the walls and gates of individual compounds or about the size of merchant plots, so those rest on other sources.

This is the same mulberry-dike-fishpond system our maps draw, and the area proportion it reports - roughly one unit of dike to one of water where the worms alone feed the fish, six or seven to four or three with other feed - follows from the feed cycle itself rather than from any modern input, so it describes the shape of a landscape that had been worked that way for centuries. The limits are that it is a 1980s development report on collective-era Chinese practice, not a historical record; that the pond depth it gives (3.5 m, drawn down in summer) reflects modern stocking and modern earth-moving and is the least premodern of its numbers; and that its figures are two worked examples and a rule of thumb, which the paper itself says is "governed by traditional practice" in the field, not regional averages.

It gives the wet paddy as a field class - the poorly drained paddy that never dries - and the direction of its conversion, which is what puts wet paddy on our maps at all. Its limits are that it is a very short aggregation of dictionary entries, carrying the distinction and the direction of change but no date or proportion; and that the conversion it documents at any scale is the Meiji-and-later national drainage program, a post-1868 undertaking outside the setting, so only the older, western-Japan beginning of the story it mentions bears on our fields.

It gives the traditional uses of the great timber bamboo - baskets, fans, food wrappings and clog coverings, the shakuhachi - which is what makes a bamboo grove on a map a working part of a farm rather than scenery. Its limits are that its uses section rests on a single citation, with the encyclopedia's own request for citations on it, so the uses are taken as common knowledge rather than as referenced findings; that the uses are undated, and the article notes that the modern clog trade has moved to another species; and that it says nothing about how big a grove was.

It gives the landform logic our foothill maps follow - dry gravel above, springs and paddy at the toe - and the physics of a fan does not change with the century. Its limits are that it carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it needs sources, so the zone terms, though standard in Japanese physical geography, are not attributed to any authority on this page; and that it is landform description only, with no dated settlement in it.

They give the form of a working river landing - the stepped bank where cargo is worked, the warehouses and merchants behind it - which is what our river towns' waterfronts are drawn from. Their limits are that one carries a notice that its sources are insufficient, the other is a stub - so neither has references of its own to carry a claim; and that the form is taken from them and no date or dimension.

It gives one clear case of a capital wall that follows the ground rather than the square - bending around lakes, hills and the river that serves as its moat - which is the form that lets our maps bend a wall where the terrain demands. Its limits are that its history and construction sections carry the encyclopedia's own requests for citations, a sharper discount than the usual one; that it is an imperial capital, so no dimension transfers to a provincial seat; and that it gives no total length for the circuit, so the 35 km figure often quoted for this wall is on no page we could read and our text says so.

It gives the division our castle plans are built on - the lord's residence and the domain's government office are two halves of one compound, one private and one where business is done - which is what a player is really asking about when they click on the inner bailey. It is generalizing across many castles and two centuries, so it describes a common arrangement rather than any particular castle's plan, and it supplies no dimensions.
We use it for the disclosure that not every temple had a resident: some held only an unqualified monk, and some had no one, a distant head priest commuting. It names the pattern and gives no share.

It gives the fallback orientation of our magistrate's manor as a rule rather than a preference - the seat sits to the north and faces south, by the regulation for a local government office and by ritual propriety - and the terms behind it mean proper rather than lucky, so the orientation is the formal one and not an auspicious one. Its limits are that it describes one surviving building of one dynasty.

It gives the open ground before a hall as a named and proportioned feature whose first stated use is drying grain and other crops, with the gatherings of the new year, the festivals, weddings and funerals second, and its width carefully matched to the height of the main hall; and it gives the half-moon pond before it holding water against drought, raising fish, watering the fields, tempering the air and standing ready against fire. It also states that the arrangement is the rule for the hall-fronted forms rather than one instance. Its limits are that its dating and normative statements carry no individual references; that it describes one regional house type with its ancestral hall on the axis, not a free-standing village shrine; that the width matched to the hall's height is the TYPE's prescriptive norm rather than a measured range, so it is a proportion to draw to and not a figure to check against; and that it gives no market and no opera on that ground.

It supplies the one measured moat width this record could read for a Chinese provincial-capital enceinte, which is what the drawn figure is checked against. Its limits are that its own citation for the figure was not followed; that Xi'an is among the largest walled circuits ever built, so its ditch is a ceiling and not an average; and that the measurement is of the ditch as it stands today after conservation.

It shows the stage real and shrine-sited but far from universal. Its limits: its own sources, Tsunoda 1971 and Gotō 1996, are closer; the 1,777 is a 1970 survey of surviving and lost stages that also counts noh and puppet stages, not a premodern prevalence; permanent stages date only from the early 1800s, farmers' theater was officially forbidden and suppressed in the Tenpō reforms, and the stages cluster in central Japan (Tokushima, Hyōgo, Nagano), with thirteen prefectures having none.

It says who had a bath of their own in the Edo period: the upper-rank samurai's shoin-style residence had a yudono, while middle and lower samurai and ordinary people washed from a tub or used the public bath, and it says what made a home bath in a city costly - digging a well, and the fuel - calling it a great luxury, though it gives no figure. Its limits are that it is covering the whole country and period in a sentence; that its sentence on who had a yudono speaks of the cities (Kyoto, Osaka, Edo and the castle towns), not of villages; that before the late Edo period the word furo meant a steam bath so the page's terms shift with the era; that the late-Edo home bath it describes was a tub (the sue-buro), and the same article says a room set aside for bathing was still rare in the Edo period, a farmhouse's tub often standing unpartitioned in a corner of the earth-floored doma; and that it says nothing of where in a samurai house or compound the yudono stood - the only baths it places are the farmhouse's (in the doma and, in the Yamakawa dictionary's entry on the same page, near the stable or privy so the used water could go to the compost) and the Heian noble house's (a tub set in a partitioned corridor, with no fixed bath room).
